summary: Correct the dictation gloss: lektieren → diktieren
rationale: The stem is glossed “schreiben lassen, lektieren”, whereas its own Preterit translation says “er liess schreiben, diktierte” and 5/12 says “diktiert”. These identify dictation and support diktieren as the intended gloss.

summary: Routine counts show writing/copying is common: 75 Preterit and 29 Infectum occurrences beyond the full rows. Counts do not license extra quotations or require decision lines.
ko-Preterit 35/21 presents a currently relevant received letter. Infectum-wa habitual writing is independently attested in MAC and Talay, distinct from Preterit-wa agent-suffix forms.
Part act. follows the inherited occupational kaṯowo convention; these nouns are not asserted to describe an ongoing writing event.
kṯawto is a feminine Nomen Actionis for writing as an activity or skill; it is distinguished from inherited Infinitiv kṯowo without creating a separate lexical sense.
Written-state predicates can combine with past copulas, as kṯuto-wa and kṯiwowa. No independent Detransitive Preterit-wa box is added on that basis.

The inherited Detransitive Preterit kṯiwo-le (LB 89) and MAC dәkṯiwile have active writers and object agreement. Their exact paradigm is disputed; no speculative move of existing examples is published.
Claims that 79/7 and 37/16 form one example are outdated relative to the supplied entry: it already has four separate Infectum examples. The actual citation leak in 79/7 is corrected.

Jan Beṯ-Şawoce English is project machine translation, not an edition translation. All semantic decisions rest on the supplied Turoyo; retained English quotations are verbatim machine translation. Only round-2 changes are encoded here.
The prose excerpts include interviews and oral restarts as well as documentary description; neither all Jan language nor all irregular forms can be assumed to be a learned written register.
I Infectum-wa and ko-Preterit are already present in round 1. Only III Infectum-wa is a new box here. kṯawto follows the round-1 Nomen Actionis analysis, not the reader’s Infinitiv label.
Jan 2.1/2 and 2.31/5217 provide finite Detransitive kṯiwi with plural patients. Bare kṯiw in 2.17/3656 and 2.32/5261 may support the singular finite form, but restarts and agreement need checking.

Actor-focused kəṯwile/kṯiwile with huwwe or ele (Jan 3.9/97; 3.17/342), kṯəwile l Gabriyel (3.17/322), and kṯiwilox (3.31/804) support round 1’s question about active writing with i-vocalism and L-suffixes. They are provisionally treated as active Preterit in decisions, never accepted as evidence of Detransitive semantics.
Recipient and topic coding includes l- addressees, ʕal- topics, b- languages/scripts, and ʕam mədone (Jan 2.17/3635). Thanks are written content; no separate idiom is established.

Jan 1.31/1379 has kṯəwto and məkṯowo in the same description of handwriting. The latter is not securely identified as Part. Pass.; no new box is inferred. Koṯawnowno, Kəṯyoleyo and the esteem-like reading at Jan 4.I/310 are not normalized or published as examples.

Is inherited LB 89/Talay 1/89 kṯiwole an object-inflected active Preterit, a written-state construction with an L-suffix, or another form? Compare MAC Besim Martyrdom of Maferyono/26; do not decide from the free translation alone.
Confirm the derivation of feminine kṯuto and kṯawto, and editorial placement of writing-skill nouns in Nomen Actionis.
At 93/40 and 93/53, can finite Detransitive forms be distinguished morphologically from Part. Pass. plus copula? Current revision uses the written-state analysis provisionally.
In JTM 5.2/16, does makṯu mean have the names recorded, rather than require each entrant to write personally? Verse 17 identifies Zin as recorder.
Check PrS drawing-command references: inherited prs 98/28 and supplied PrS 37/25 quote the same wording.
107/10 has flagged translation alignment and uncertain kṯuwwanne segmentation; verify against the edition before quoting it.
At Jan 1.36/1535, what is written, and whose name is involved? Establish the legal act before admitting a technical sense.
At Jan 2.12/2871, parse kṯəwolan and its actor/object suffixes; the machine translation’s second-person writer is not established by -lan.
Check makṯəwole after Man at Jan 1.21/1004: direct writing with a fused interrogative or stem III? It is withheld rather than used as a new form.
Identify məkṯowo at Jan 1.31/1379 and Kəṯyoleyo at Jan 3.15/188; check the source or recording before assigning a box.
Do actor-focused kṯiwile/kəṯwile and -lox variants represent a distinct active construction? Compare the disputed inherited LB 89 example already questioned in round 1.
Resolve person and aspect of kəṯwulle (Jan 2.17/3628), kəṯwowalox (2.17/3631), and kəṯwatte (2.17/3643); resolve kəṯwiwo aʕle (4.I/310) without relying on the machine esteem gloss.
At Jan 1.6/87, confirm expanded kṯəwle spelling and how the following səyomo phrase is coordinated; at Jan 3.37/1080 check duplicated-looking -nowno.
Restore the accusative ending in den (Blumen) Namen
rationale: Name requires the weak accusative ending after den. The supplied edition has the complete form Namen.

summary: Gifts and incidents denote the information written down about them; these content extensions remain ordinary writing.

Administrative writing of information about people or books, professional petition writing, and institutional publishing remain participant/construction extensions of ordinary writing. Inventory registration is not round-1 1b, which is specifically assignment of a person to a service location.
Administrative inventory registration is expressed by the causative makṯəwilan, with repeated negative and then affirmative clauses; complements are the registered books.
Active-shaped kkoṯəw predicates written content, continuing the inherited LB 230 sign example rather than establishing a new Detransitive paradigm.
